source.title_on_document: My Way or the AI Way? How Autonomy Frustration Undermines Creative Performance Through Editing AI Advice

supplement.where: Online Supporting Information section of the Wiley article (p. 14, 'Supporting Information'); data at OSF https://osf.io/qyvj8/overview (p. 5, p. 10)
supplement.holds: Figure S1: box plot of DAT scores across the human, human-ChatGPT-4, and ChatGPT-4 groups with Tukey HSD group differences (the only place the human-alone vs human-with-AI-advice comparison is shown); Table S1: mediation results without covariates. The main text prints no mean or SD of DAT for the no-AI group.

paper_design_summary: A qualitative prestudy interviewed 26 German graduate working students about autonomy when using AI. In the main study, 377 students from three German universities completed the Divergent Association Task (DAT) and chose for themselves whether to receive a fixed ChatGPT-4-generated 10-word DAT solution that they could edit (222 chose AI advice, 155 did not); the paper relates self-reported autonomy frustration and the number of edited words to the computed DAT score within the AI-advice group, and compares DAT across the human-alone, human-with-AI-advice, and ChatGPT-alone groups in a footnote. A separate manipulation-check sample (120 analyzed, 88 who chose AI advice) reported decision-making autonomy for the DAT with and without AI advice.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing assigned; qualitative interviews about attitudes, autonomy, and authenticity when using AI.
assignment.quote: we conducted a preliminary interview study (Gibson 2016).

arms.name: Interviewees
arms.description: Graduate students with AI experience interviewed for 10 to 15 min

participants.who: Graduate students at a large German business school working at least 20 h per week as working students; all had used LLMs such as ChatGPT.
participants.quote: Our sample included 26 participants (17 females and nine males) who were 24.4 years old on average (SD = 1.8).

ai_tool.name_model: Not applicable (interviews about general LLM use such as ChatGPT)
ai_tool.how_used: No AI used in the study; participants described their own AI use.

task.description: Semistructured interview on attitudes toward AI and sense of autonomy and authenticity when using AI for tasks.

studies.label: Main study (DAT with optional, self-selected ChatGPT-4 advice)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomly assigned. Participants chose whether to receive a fixed AI-generated DAT solution (10 words from ChatGPT-4) that they could edit, or to generate their own 10 words.
assignment.quote: participants were given the option to receive AI-generated advice from ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI 2023). Participants who chose to receive the AI advice (N=222) were presented with a set of 10 AI-generated words

arms.name: AI advice (self-selected)
arms.description: Shown a fixed set of 10 ChatGPT-4-generated words (horizon, planet, notebook, honesty, chimpanzee, cake, plateau, opera, airplane, gloves) and allowed to edit any number before submitting.

arms.name: No AI advice (self-selected)
arms.description: Opted out of AI advice and generated their own 10 words.

participants.exclusions: 397 recruited; 20 excluded for missing data, leaving 377. No Mahalanobis outliers. The paper does not say which arm the 20 excluded people had chosen. The mediation analysis uses only the 222 who chose AI advice.
participants.who: Students from three large German universities, mostly in part-time (dual) degree courses while employed; course credit; 77.5% female; mean age 24.84; mean 26.19 h work per week.
participants.quote: We excluded 20 participants due to missing data, resulting in a final sample of 377 participants
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 4.1.1; arm counts p. 6, Section 4.1.1

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (one pre-generated DAT solution, chosen from 100 generated solutions as the one closest to their mean score, footnote 3)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants who opted in saw one fixed 10-word AI solution and could edit any number of the words; no live interaction with the chatbot.

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): name 10 single nouns as different from each other as possible; scored by computed semantic distance of the first seven valid words.

outcomes.name: DAT score (creative task performance)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT score: transformed average pairwise semantic distance among the first seven valid words, computed by algorithm (p. 6, Section 4.1.2.2). Robustness: mediation without covariates in Supporting Information Table S1 (not in this PDF).

contrasts.reported: No direct statistic for this pair in the main text. Footnote 5 gives both groups relative to ChatGPT-4 alone: human-alone dM = -7.94, 95% CI [-9.36, -6.52]; human-ChatGPT dM = -4.08, 95% CI [-5.51, -2.65]; one-way ANOVA F(2, 402) = 87.24, p < 0.001. The Tukey HSD comparison of human vs human-ChatGPT is in Supporting Information Figure S1 (not in this PDF). Arms self-selected. AI-advice group DAT M = 82.87, SD = 4.51 (Table 1, N = 222); no-AI group mean not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, footnote 5; p. 7, Table 1; p. 14, Supporting Information

contrasts.reported: Human-ChatGPT collaboration group scored lower than ChatGPT-4 alone: dM = -4.08, 95% CI [-5.51, -2.65], p < 0.001 (post hoc after ANOVA F(2, 402) = 87.24, p < 0.001). ChatGPT-4 alone: 100 solutions, M = 85.62, SD = 3.42 (footnote 3).

contrasts.treatment_arm: More words edited (extent of editing, 0-10), within the AI-advice group
contrasts.control_arm: Fewer words edited, within the AI-advice group
contrasts.reported: Path b, extent of editing on DAT: B = -0.621, SE = 0.053, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.727, -0.515]; correlation r = -0.62 (Table 1). Autonomy frustration on DAT (path c'): B = 0.100, SE = 0.208, p = 0.630; indirect effect via editing B = -0.403, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.721, -0.084]; R2 = 0.404. N = 222, unstandardized, covariates gender, age, education, weekly working hours, prior ChatGPT use. Observational association, not an arm contrast.

studies.label: Manipulation check (separate sample; autonomy with vs without AI advice)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not randomized. Of the analyzed sample, 88 participants who chose AI advice completed the DAT with and without AI-generated advice and rated decision-making autonomy for each; the order of conditions is not stated.
assignment.quote: We examined whether the 88 participants (77.3% identified as female and the rest as male, Mage = 24.7, SD = 1.87) who chose to receive AI advice in the DAT differed in their reported decisionmaking autonomy

arms.name: DAT with AI advice
arms.description: Same 88 participants, condition with AI-generated advice

arms.name: DAT without AI advice
arms.description: Same 88 participants, condition without AI-generated advice

participants.exclusions: 131 recruited; 11 failed at least one of two attention checks; no Mahalanobis outliers; 120 analyzed. The within-person autonomy comparison uses the 88 who chose AI advice.
participants.who: Students from a large German business school; 76.7% female; mean age 24.5.
participants.quote: We recruited 131 students from a large German business school. Of these, 11 failed at least one of two attention check items

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (AI-generated DAT advice; presumably the same fixed solution, not stated for this sample)
ai_tool.how_used: AI-generated DAT advice shown in the with-AI condition.

task.description: Divergent Association Task completed with and without AI-generated advice; only self-reported decision-making autonomy is reported.

outcomes.name: Self-reported decision-making autonomy during the creativity task
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Three items adapted from Morgeson and Humphrey (2006), 5-point Likert; omega 0.77 without, 0.86 with AI advice. No DAT scores reported for this sample.

contrasts.reported: With AI advice M = 3.07, SD = 1.19 vs without M = 4.29, SD = 0.64; t(87) = 9.28, p < 0.001, d = 0.99; N = 88 (paired).

company_involvement.description: Authors at Technical University of Munich; no funding reported (p. 10, Funding). ChatGPT-4 used as a tool only.

eligibility.reason: In the main study (377 analyzed), participants chose for themselves whether to receive the ChatGPT-4 advice (222 yes, 155 no; p. 6, Section 4.1.1), so AI assistance was self-selected, not randomly assigned. The DAT score is computed on the output (criterion 3 met), and the sample exceeds 50 people. The manipulation-check study reports only self-reported autonomy, and the prestudy is qualitative interviews. Non-random comparison of people with and without AI goes to observational context (design quasi_people).

one_line_finding: Among 222 students who chose fixed ChatGPT-4 advice on the DAT, editing more AI words predicted lower DAT scores (B = -0.621, SE = 0.053; p. 7, Table 2), and the self-selected human-with-AI group scored 4.08 points below ChatGPT-4 alone but less far below than the human-alone group (7.94 points; p. 10, footnote 5).
open_questions: The ANOVA in footnote 5 has F(2, 402), implying 405 observations across three groups, but the size of the ChatGPT-4-alone group in that ANOVA is not stated (footnote 3 describes 100 generated solutions). The AI-advice group mean in Table 1 (82.87) plus the printed difference to ChatGPT-4 alone (4.08) does not match the footnote 3 mean of 85.62; the ChatGPT-alone reference in the ANOVA may differ. Supporting Information Figure S1 may resolve this.
Whether the 20 excluded participants in the main study had chosen AI advice or not is not stated.
In the manipulation check, the order of the with-AI and without-AI DAT conditions is not stated, nor whether the same fixed AI solution was used.
notes: Candidates record lists an SSRN version (abstract 5233181); this form uses the journal version on file. The ethics statement mentions 'three studies' (prestudy, main study, manipulation check). Extent of editing (number of AI words changed, 0-10) is a behavioral process measure, not a creativity outcome, and is not listed as an outcome. Autonomy frustration (METUX TENS-task, 3 items, omega 0.70, 7-point) is self-reported and measured only in the AI-advice group.
